implementation_constraints: reads one JSON value from stdin, prints one line, exits 0

unresolved_intent.decision: Fixed allowlist of read-only tool names — read, glob, grep, ls, list, search, websearch, webfetch, fetch, notebookread, todoread — matched case-insensitively after trimming; everything else falls into the unknown-tool branch.
unresolved_intent.rationale: The SPEC names the family by kind (file reader, text search, directory listing, notebook reader, web fetch/search) but never enumerates the host's actual tool names. An allowlist is the only fail-closed reading: an unrecognised name is treated as potentially write-capable, so a missing synonym costs a false BLOCK (safe) rather than a false ALLOW (the one failure the subsystem must never have).

unresolved_intent.ir_region: shell read-only command vocabulary and subcommand handling (AC-GH-05)
unresolved_intent.decision: Default-deny allowlist of reader programs (cat/head/grep/rg/ls/find/diff/jq/awk/sort/…); `git` is admitted only for a read-only subcommand set (show, log, diff, status, cat-file, ls-files, blame, …); `python`/`node` are admitted as programs but are still blocked by the redirection, write-flag and command-substitution checks whenever they touch a golden.
unresolved_intent.rationale: The SPEC demands `treat the command as a WRITE unless every part of it is a recognised read-only operation` without giving a vocabulary. Multi-purpose programs like `git` read under one subcommand and write under another, so program-level allowlisting alone would leak `git checkout -- x.approved`; requiring a subcommand match keeps the default-deny posture intact at one more level.

unresolved_intent.ir_region: scope of the marker test for the shell tool — `command` string vs. the whole `tool_input`
unresolved_intent.decision: A shell call is allowed early only when the marker appears neither in the `command` string nor anywhere else in `tool_input`; if the marker is present anywhere, the command must be proven read-only to pass. When `command` is present but is not a string, the call blocks if the marker appears anywhere in `tool_input`.
unresolved_intent.rationale: The SPEC scopes the shell rule to the `command` string, but a host may also carry paths in sibling fields (cwd, description, files). Extending the trigger to the full argument object, while keeping the read-only proof on the command text, closes that gap without weakening AC-GH-03 (a genuine `cat x.approved` still passes).

unresolved_intent.ir_region: redirection, substitution and pipeline detection in the absence of a real shell parser
unresolved_intent.decision: A regex flags `>`/`>>`/`n>`/`>|`/`<>` redirections and a literal check flags `$(`, backticks and `>(`; the line is then tokenized with `shlex(punctuation_chars=True)` and split on `| || && ; & |&`, and EVERY resulting stage must independently prove read-only. Any `shlex` ValueError (unbalanced quotes) blocks.
unresolved_intent.rationale: Implementing a POSIX shell grammar is out of proportion for a text/structure guardrail, but `starts with a reader` is explicitly insufficient per AC-GH-05. Per-stage proof makes `cat g.approved | tee other.approved` block on the tee stage, and treating unparsable input as a block preserves fail-closed rather than degrading to a substring heuristic.

unresolved_intent.ir_region: `tool_input` absent, null, or non-object; leading env-assignments and wrapper commands
unresolved_intent.decision: A missing or `null` `tool_input` is normalised to `{}` and allowed for a non-golden call, while a present-but-non-object `tool_input` blocks as an unexpected shape (AC-GH-07). Inside a stage, leading `VAR=value` assignments and wrappers (`env`, `command`, `sudo`, `nohup`, `time`, `exec`) are stripped before the program is identified, and a stage that is empty after stripping is treated as NOT read-only.
unresolved_intent.rationale: The SPEC calls `tool_input` an object holding arguments but does not say whether omission is malformed; a tool with no arguments cannot name a golden, so blocking it would be noise, whereas a string or list in that slot is genuinely the wrong shape. Stripping wrappers prevents `env cat x.approved` from being misread as an unknown program (false block) while the empty-stage rule keeps a bare `sudo` from being misread as safe (false allow).
